passages.text: If Industry Analysts Disappeared Tomorrow, Could AI Fill the Gap? What AI Can Accelerate - and Why Human Judgment, Relationships, and Market Influence Still Matter AI can process enormous volumes of information, identify patterns, and generate insights at remarkable speed. But could it replace the judgment, relationships, market context, and influence industry analysts bring to technology decisions? Exploring that question reveals where AI may transform the analyst ecosystem - and where human expertise remains indispensable.

AI can carry more of the information burden. It cannot manufacture independent market perspective, own a relationship, or assume accountability for a recommendation. Forward Perspectives Deborah Frazier Why AI Cannot Replace Analyst Relations - But Can Make It Better AI can carry more of the information burden. It cannot manufacture independent market perspective, build trusted relationships, or assume accountability for a recommendation.

AI is forcing business leaders, industry analysts, and Analyst Relations teams to reconsider how market intelligence is created and applied. The question is no longer whether AI should be used. It should. The more important question is where AI creates genuine advantage, and where relying on it too heavily could separate companies from the people, original insight, and outside perspective they need to compete.

If Industry Analysts Disappeared, Could AI Fill the Gap? Technology companies would still have sales data, customer interviews, competitive research, product reviews, and enormous amounts of public information. AI could compare vendors, explain categories, assemble shortlists, and recommend products based on stated requirements. But something essential would be missing: an independent group continually speaking with buyers and vendors, testing company claims, and identifying patterns across the broader market.

Every company sees the market through the boundaries of its own experience. It rarely hears from buyers who never considered it, eliminated it early, misunderstood its positioning, or chose another category entirely. Industry analysts occupy a different position. Through research, inquiries, briefings, advisory work, and buyer conversations, they recognize patterns no individual vendor can see from inside its own organization. They may discover that buyers distrust a common claim, require evidence vendors are not providing, or define a problem differently from the companies attempting to solve it.

Without that external perspective, companies risk becoming highly efficient at analyzing, and reinforcing their own assumptions. AI Depends on Original Human Insight Analyst research, market evaluations, category definitions, and independent points of view create original information that AI can organize and connect. If analysts stopped producing that work, AI would not simply take over from the same foundation. That foundation would gradually shrink. Public information could become increasingly dominated by promotional content, vendor claims, and material generated from previous AI summaries.

Visibility could begin to look like credibility. AI can organize information, compare claims, monitor competitors, summarize research, and surface possible patterns. These capabilities can make analysts and AR professionals significantly more effective. But AI cannot interpret information it never receives. It cannot earn the trust that causes a buyer or executive to disclose what is truly influencing a decision. It may identify a pattern, but an experienced person must still determine whether that pattern is meaningful, misleading, or incomplete.

Why Analyst Relations Remains Essential Access to analyst feedback does not automatically tell a company what to do with it. A repeated question could indicate unclear positioning, insufficient evidence, changing buyer priorities, a new research direction, or simply a standard question being asked of every vendor. Senior AR professionals understand the analysts, the company’s history, and what was said, or left unsaid, during an interaction. They interpret feedback in context, prepare executives, manage trusted relationships, and translate relevant intelligence into practical business decisions.

AI can support that work. It should not own it. How a Personal Question Helped Shape Forward For me, this was never merely theoretical. My husband, Gary, has spent more than 30 years in Analyst Relations. When he was laid off and spent five months searching for his next opportunity, we repeatedly encountered an unsettling question: Could AI replace experienced AR professionals?

The possibility was frightening - professionally and personally. But searching for an honest answer led us somewhere more constructive. Gary understood how scattered research, interaction histories, analyst feedback, internal documents, and institutional memory affect AR teams. Drawing on more than two decades of experience building businesses, sales systems, and growth strategies, I saw the operating and technology challenge underneath it.

We originally expected to build Forward together. When Gary accepted a professional opportunity that was too important for our family to decline, Forward had to become larger than either of us. It needed a system that could help experienced practitioners work from a stronger foundation without removing human judgment, relationships, or accountability. That principle shaped Forward’s senior-only delivery model and its interconnected intelligence ecosystem: the Forward Intelligence Library, AI-Enabled Intelligence Knowledge Base, and Sales Engine. Together, they connect thought leadership, market intelligence, practitioner expertise, and audience insight in a system designed to become more valuable over time.

The Forward Intelligence Library extends that purpose to the broader AR community. It gives analysts, AR practitioners, executives, and cross-functional leaders a permanent, AI-searchable home for practical knowledge and informed perspectives. Valuable ideas, and the professionals behind them, should remain discoverable instead of disappearing in a social feed or aging unnoticed in a forgotten blog archive.

The issue is not simply whether your product uses AI. passages.text: Storytelling Analyst Briefings Influence Mechanics Series Explore how effective analyst briefings combine narrative clarity, relevant evidence and disciplined preparation - helping analysts understand what matters, why it is different and where it fits in the market. Storytelling Analyst Briefings Forward AR Experts Analyst Briefings are built on one principle: analysts reward clarity, discipline, and substance - not theatrics, volume, or marketing gloss. Our approach transforms briefings from one‑off presentations into strategic moments of influence that strengthen perception, reinforce narrative consistency, and build long‑term analyst trust . Every briefing is designed, prepared, and delivered with senior‑level precision.

At the core of our methodology is strategic clarity. Analysts expect vendors to articulate what they do, why it matters, and how they deliver measurable outcomes. Forward AR Experts ensures every briefing opens with a crisp, differentiated narrative that anchors the conversation and eliminates ambiguity. This narrative is not a slide; it is a strategic asset, one aligned across executives, product leaders, and spokespeople. This directly connects to Narrative Development and the broader AR Operating System .

The second pillar is evidence‑backed credibility. Analysts are trained to look past claims and assess the strength of proof. Our briefings integrate validated customer outcomes, product performance data, competitive wins, and measurable impact. We eliminate inflated statements and replace them with defensible evidence that stands up under scrutiny. This approach signals maturity and operational strength, reinforcing the vendor’s position in the market. It aligns with Evidence‑Backed Differentiation.

The third component is executive fluency. Analysts evaluate not only the content but the command and confidence of the leaders delivering it . Forward AR Experts prepares executives to speak with clarity, depth, and strategic coherence without drifting into marketing language or over‑promising . We coach leaders to answer tough questions transparently, articulate product direction with precision, and demonstrate alignment across the organization. This is a defining maturity signal and a core part of Executive Influence .

The fourth pillar is briefing discipline. High‑performing vendors do not improvise. They follow a structured briefing flow that respects analyst time, anticipates their questions, and delivers the right level of detail. Our briefing framework ensures every session is paced, purposeful, and aligned to analyst expectations. We eliminate unnecessary slides, reduce noise, and focus on the insights analysts value most : clarity, differentiation, and evidence.

The fifth component is engagement readiness. A briefing is not an isolated event; it is part of a year‑round rhythm of influence. Forward AR Experts ensures vendors show up prepared, with updated narratives, fresh evidence, aligned spokespeople, and a clear understanding of the analyst’s recent research and perspective. This readiness signals maturity and strengthens trust over time.

Finally, our briefings emphasize strategic follow‑through. Analysts remember vendors who close the loop, provide requested materials quickly, and maintain momentum after the meeting. We build follow‑up discipline into the process, ensuring every interaction reinforces credibility and strengthens the relationship. items.title: Analyst Confidence Curve
items.summary: Explore how analyst confidence rises or falls through accumulated signals, and how narrative clarity, credible evidence and consistent execution turn uncertainty into lasting trust.

passages.text: Confidence Analyst Confidence Curve Influence Mechanics Series Explore how analyst confidence rises or falls through accumulated signals, and how narrative clarity, credible evidence and consistent execution turn uncertainty into lasting trust. Confidence Analyst Confidence Curve The Analyst Confidence Curve maps how analyst conviction strengthens or weakens based on the consistency, clarity, and credibility of the signals a vendor sends over time. Confidence is not built in a single briefing; it is accumulated through a sequence of interactions, each one reinforcing or eroding the analyst’s belief in the vendor’s stability, maturity, and ability to deliver. The curve reveals the inflection points where uncertainty converts into trust, and where trust can quickly collapse.

At the foundation of the curve is narrative clarity. Analysts begin forming confidence the moment they understand, with precision, what a vendor does, why it matters, and how it delivers outcomes. When the narrative is crisp, aligned, and reinforced across executives and functions, the curve begins to rise. When the narrative is vague, shifting, or overloaded with marketing language , the curve flattens. Narrative clarity is the first accelerant of confidence and ties directly to Narrative Development.

The second driver is evidence density, the volume and quality of proof supporting the narrative. Analysts are trained to discount claims and reward verification. Customer outcomes, product performance data, competitive wins, and measurable impact all add weight to the curve. Each piece of evidence increases the analyst’s conviction that the vendor can deliver on its promises. Thin, inconsistent, or inflated evidence causes the curve to stall or decline. This is the core of Evidence‑Backed Differentiation.

The third force shaping the curve is executive behavior. Analysts evaluate leaders as much as products. Executives who communicate with clarity, transparency, and grounded confidence accelerate the curve. Executives who overclaim , deflect, or rely on scripted talking points introduce friction. Analysts interpret executive maturity as organizational maturity, and executive instability as organizational instability. This is why Executive Influence is a defining maturity signal.

The fourth component is engagement timing. Confidence grows when interactions are well‑timed, proactive, and aligned to analyst needs. Vendors who show up only during evaluations flatten the curve. Vendors who maintain a steady rhythm of briefings , inquiries, updates, and evidence delivery create upward momentum. Timing signals operational discipline, and discipline builds trust. As these four forces work together, the Analyst Confidence Curve reaches its inflection point: the moment analysts shift from cautious observation to active advocacy. At this point, analysts begin referencing the vendor more positively, comparing them more favorably, and incorporating them more confidently into research. This is where influence compounds.

But, the curve can also decline. Confidence erodes when vendors send conflicting signals: inconsistent narratives, weak evidence, executive misalignment, roadmap surprises, or reactive engagement. The decline is often faster than the rise, because analysts interpret inconsistency as instability. The Analyst Confidence Curve is ultimately a model of predictable influence. Vendors who understand it operate with intention: they build clarity early, reinforce it with evidence, show up with strong executives, and maintain a steady rhythm of engagement. When these elements align, analyst confidence becomes durable, and durable confidence becomes market advantage.

items.title: Analyst Relations Strategy Narrative
items.summary: What separates a strong analyst relations strategy from a weak one? A narrative built for analysts, not prospects.

passages.text: Clear Communication Your Analyst Relations Strategy Needs a Narrative Built for Analysts, Not Prospects Strategy & Market Positioning Series Explore how clarity, consistency and credibility help your company earn a lasting place in analysts’ minds, and turn a memorable, repeatable narrative into influence and competitive advantage. Clear Communication I'm a content and product marketer who's spent the last 10+ years helping B2B SaaS companies explain complicated products to people who don't have time to be confused.

Contribute to Our Library Check Out Our Library Tara Porter Dill Product Marketing Manager Tara Porter | LinkedIn Your Analyst Relations Strategy Needs a Narrative Built for Analysts, Not Prospects Analysts sit in a different room than customers. The narrative that works there comes from product marketing and analyst relations building it side by side.

An analyst relations (AR) lead spends weeks lining up a briefing , only to watch the analyst nod through every slide and ask, at the end, how this is different from three other vendors already on their list. The deck answered every question a prospect might ask. It never answered that one. So what was the problem?

Messaging written for customers doesn't do the same job as messaging built for analysts. That's why building an analyst relations strategy starts with product marketing and AR shaping a narrative for the analyst audience, rather than repurposing the deck built for prospects. Why Customer Messaging Fails as an Analyst Relations Strategy A customer wants proof the product fits their situation. An analyst wants a framework for comparing this company to everyone else covering the same space. Hand an analyst the same deck you gave a prospect, and you've handed them the job of translating a sales pitch into an industry analysis. Some analysts do that work well. Plenty don't.

Gary Frazier, director of analyst relations at Icertis, put it this way: "A deck built for customers focuses on why we're the best or the first to meet their current needs. A deck built for analysts has to tell a bigger story: where we sit in the broader market, what trends are driving customers to invest in this kind of technology, and where we're headed to meet future challenges, not just today's needs."

That bigger story, the market context and the trends behind it, is what a customer deck skips and an analyst deck can't. A customer deck says "we help you close deals faster." An analyst deck says something closer to "the market is moving from point tools to consolidated platforms, and here's the decision we made to get ahead of that shift." Same company, same product, a completely different argument.

Why This Takes Both Product Marketing and Analyst Relations Product marketing has access to what the product team built and why. Analyst relations has access to how the market reacts to what's already been said about it. Neither half is complete without the other. Frazier described what that partnership looks like day to day: "My product marketing managers have been my closest partners. They help me build content for briefings, and they're integral to the RFI response and demo development process. They often act as my liaison to the product team, translating technical detail into business terms and identifying the competitive differentiators behind new innovations. In turn, I make sure my PMMs have access to key research and analysts, and I feed market insights back to them at every opportunity."

Skip either half and the gap shows up fast: sharp on the technology and thin on why the market should care, or the reverse, a compelling market story with nothing underneath it an analyst can verify. Finding the Point of View That's Genuinely Yours A strong analyst narrative starts with a genuine point of view, something analysts haven't already heard from every other vendor in the category.

Every company claims it's innovative. Every company claims it's customer-obsessed. Every company claims it's built to scale. None of that helps an analyst distinguish one vendor from the next. Start by asking product and engineering what they built differently on purpose, not what they built better. "Better" is an opinion, and a competitor can claim their version is better too, which turns the conversation into a fight neither side wins.

"Different on purpose" points to a decision your team made deliberately, one another vendor would not have made the same way. Say your team decided to build one unified data model, skipping the usual patchwork of stitched-together tools. That's a decision someone can point to, explain, and defend. It becomes something an analyst can repeat accurately, since it describes a fact about how the product works, not a judgment about how good it is. The claim that comes out of it reads something like: "We built one data model, so customers don't need middleware to keep records in sync, where most competitors bolted three systems together instead."

A real differentiator is something no competitor could also say. "We help businesses grow faster" could come from almost any vendor, so it doesn't count. If your claim could double as a competitor's tagline, you haven't found it yet. Everyone Claims AI. Be Specific About What Yours Does. Generic messaging gets almost funny once you look at how companies describe AI. Every vendor pitch these days claims to be AI-powered, and the ones that skip that word swap in "intelligent" or "built on the latest models." Repeat a phrase enough times and it stops carrying any meaning. It becomes wallpaper. I'd guess most analysts could finish that sentence before the vendor does.

Specificity fixes this. Here's what that looks like in practice: Swap "AI-powered forecasting" for what the model predicts and on what timeline. Example: "Predicts inventory shortfalls three weeks out, using live supplier shipment data." Replace "intelligent automation" with the exact decision the system makes without a person, and where a person steps back in. Example: "Automatically approves invoices under $500 and flags anything higher for manager review."

passages.text: Pulse AR Program Health Check Program Excellence Series The AR Program Health Check provides a focused, senior-led evaluation of your strategy, relationships, positioning and execution - revealing what is working, where credibility or influence may be at risk and what to prioritize next. Pulse AR Program Health Check Most analyst relations programs don’t fail because of a single issue. They fail because of a series of small misalignments, outdated assumptions, and missing disciplines that compound over time. Vendors often believe their AR program is performing “well enough,” only to be surprised by evaluation outcomes, analyst feedback, or competitive movement they didn’t anticipate.

That’s why every vendor, regardless of size, category, or maturity - needs a structured AR Program Health Check. It’s the fastest, most accurate way to understand whether your program is aligned to analyst expectations , market realities, and the internal disciplines required to influence perception. In my work with technology companies, I’ve seen how transformative a Health Check can be. It reveals blind spots. It exposes gaps . It clarifies priorities. And it gives vendors a roadmap for strengthening analyst trust and improving evaluation performance .

A Health Check Reveals Narrative Misalignment. Most vendors assume their narrative is clear and differentiated. Analysts often disagree. A Health Check identifies where messaging is inconsistent, overly complex, or disconnected from category expectations. It ensures the story analysts hear is the story you intend to tell - grounded in evidence, not aspiration. It Exposes Roadmap and Strategy Gaps. Analysts evaluate vendors based on execution discipline , prioritization, and strategic clarity. A Health Check highlights where roadmaps lack rationale, where strategy is unclear, or where internal teams are misaligned. These gaps are often invisible internally but obvious to analysts.

It Evaluates Customer Evidence. Customer proof is one of the most influential components of analyst perception. A Health Check assesses whether your evidence is strong enough, specific enough, and aligned to the outcomes analysts expect. It also identifies where evidence is missing and how to build it systematically. It Assesses Executive Readiness. Executives play a critical role in analyst perception, but only when they’re prepared. A Health Check evaluates whether leaders are aligned, confident, and equipped to speak to category dynamics, customer outcomes, and strategic priorities. When executives are unprepared, analysts notice immediately.

It Identifies Engagement Cadence Issues. Analysts expect consistent, proactive engagement, not reactive outreach tied to evaluations. A Health Check reveals whether your cadence is strategic, whether you’re engaging the right analysts, and whether your interactions reinforce the narrative or dilute it. It Highlights Process and Operational Gaps. Strong AR programs operate with discipline. A Health Check uncovers where processes are missing, inconsistent, or overly dependent on individuals rather than systems. These operational gaps often explain why programs struggle to scale or maintain consistency.

What Should Vendors Do Now? To strengthen AR program performance, companies should: • Conduct a structured AR Program Health Check at least annually • Align narrative, roadmap, and customer evidence to analyst expectations • Prepare executives with consistent messaging and category context • Establish a proactive engagement cadence with the right analysts • Treat AR program health as a strategic priority, not a reactive task

Contribute Your Own Article Explore Our Library Gary Frazier Icertis Analyst Relations Director Gary Frazier | LinkedIn Analyst Relations Cross-Functional Leadership Analyst Relations has evolved far beyond the coordination of briefings , inquiries, and evaluation cycles. Today, AR leadership requires a level of strategic judgment, narrative clarity, and organizational influence that cannot be met through execution alone. As analyst expectations rise, the companies that succeed are those with AR leaders who operate as strategic partners - individuals who bring discipline, foresight, and a deep understanding of how analysts interpret markets, competitors, and executive behavior.

At its core, AR leadership is the ability to translate complex internal realities into narratives analysts trust. This requires more than messaging. It requires discernment: knowing what to say, when to say it, and how analysts will interpret it within the broader context of their research. Analysts are not simply listening for updates; they are evaluating consistency, maturity, and the company’s ability to deliver on its commitments. AR leaders must therefore maintain a steady cadence of engagement that reinforces clarity rather than noise.

A defining characteristic of strong AR leadership is the ability to anticipate. Analysts rarely ask questions at face value. Their inquiries reflect deeper signals - shifts in market perception, competitive pressure, or concerns about execution. Effective AR leaders read these signals early and guide internal teams to respond with confidence and alignment. This anticipatory posture transforms AR from a reactive function into a strategic asset.

Equally important is the ability to influence cross‑functional partners. AR leaders sit at the intersection of product, marketing, communications, and executive leadership. They must ensure that every contributor understands the analyst perspective and the implications of inconsistent narratives. This requires diplomacy, clarity, and the authority to push for alignment when internal priorities diverge. Without this internal leadership, even the strongest external strategy will falter.

Another hallmark of mature AR leadership is methodological discipline . Analysts expect consistency: consistent narratives, consistent engagement, consistent follow‑through. A structured methodology - one that defines how narratives are shaped, how analysts are prioritized, and how interactions are prepared - creates the predictability analysts associate with high‑performing companies. This discipline builds trust over time, turning skepticism into confidence and confidence into advocacy.

Finally, AR leadership demands a steady hand during moments of change. Whether navigating new product categories , leadership transitions , or competitive shifts, analysts look to AR leaders for clarity and stability. The ability to guide executives through analyst‑facing conversations, prepare them for difficult questions, and reinforce the company’s long‑term vision is a critical differentiator . In these moments, AR leaders are not simply facilitators - they are strategic advisors shaping how the market understands the company’s trajectory.

In a landscape where analyst influence continues to grow, AR leadership is no longer optional. It is a strategic necessity. Companies that invest in senior‑level AR leadership gain more than improved evaluations -they gain a partner who brings discipline, judgment, and a deep understanding of how to build lasting analyst advocacy. And in a market defined by perception as much as performance, that leadership becomes a competitive advantage.

Submit Your Own Article Visit Our Library Gary Frazier Icertis Analyst Relations Director Gary Frazier | LinkedIn The AR Operating System The AR Operating System is the disciplined framework that transforms Analyst Relations from a reactive function into a predictable, repeatable, and strategically aligned engine of influence. It provides the structure, governance, and operational rigor required to ensure every analyst interaction, from briefings to evaluations, reinforces the company’s narrative, credibility, and long‑term market position. The AR Operating System is not a set of tasks; it is the backbone of a mature, high‑performing AR program .

At its core, the AR Operating System establishes strategic clarity. Analysts expect vendors to articulate a crisp, differentiated narrative that explains what the company does, why it matters, and how it delivers measurable outcomes. Without clarity, AR becomes a cycle of inconsistent messaging and reactive storytelling. With clarity, AR becomes a strategic force that aligns internal teams and shapes external perception. This clarity becomes the foundation for every engagement and directly connects to narrative development and evidence‑backed differentiation.

The second component is governance: the processes, roles, and decision frameworks that ensure AR operates with consistency and discipline. Governance defines who speaks to analysts, how information is validated, how claims are substantiated, and how cross‑functional teams collaborate. It eliminates ambiguity, reduces risk, and ensures the company shows up with maturity . Strong governance signals to analysts that the vendor is aligned, credible, and operationally sound.

The third component is engagement rhythm. High‑performing AR programs do not rely on sporadic briefings or last‑minute evaluation prep. They operate on a structured cadence of proactive interactions, timely updates, and strategic touchpoints that build momentum throughout the year. This rhythm ensures analysts receive the right information at the right time, not too early, not too late. It also ensures the company stays top‑of‑mind as categories evolve and competitive narratives shift. Engagement rhythm is the operational heartbeat of the AR Operating System.

The fourth component is evidence creation. Analysts increasingly expect proof, not promises. The AR Operating System embeds evidence generation into the company’s operating model - customer outcomes, product performance, competitive wins, and measurable impact. Evidence becomes a continuous output, not a scramble during evaluations. This discipline strengthens credibility and directly supports Gartner MQ & Forrester Wave Readiness.

The fifth component is evaluation readiness. The AR Operating System ensures the company is always prepared for major evaluations, not just during submission windows. It aligns product, marketing, customer success, and executives around the requirements, expectations, and scoring logic of each framework. This readiness reduces stress, eliminates last‑minute chaos, and improves outcomes by ensuring the company shows up consistently strong.

The final component is measurement. AR leaders must demonstrate impact - on perception, narrative adoption, competitive positioning, and evaluation performance. The AR Operating System includes a measurement framework that tracks progress, identifies gaps , and informs strategic decisions. Measurement turns AR from an activity‑driven function into a results‑driven discipline. The AR Operating System is the foundation of AR excellence. It brings structure, clarity, and repeatability to a function that too often relies on intuition and ad‑hoc execution. When implemented with discipline, it becomes one of the most powerful levers for shaping analyst perception and driving long‑term market leadership.

It's About Leading a Cross-Functional Team and Earning Their Trust: When AR Performs Well, the Whole Company Looks Stronger - MQs, Waves, MarketScapes, etc., are evaluations of the company as a whole, not the AR program. Shape Forward AR Experts Strategic Maturity AR Strategic Maturity is the evolution from reactive, activity‑driven Analyst Relations to a disciplined, executive‑aligned function that shapes perception, strengthens credibility, and drives long‑term market influence. Mature AR programs don’t simply manage briefings or evaluations; they operate as strategic engines that align narrative, category, and analyst expectations to accelerate business outcomes. Strategic maturity is not defined by volume, headcount, or tools; it is defined by clarity, consistency, and the ability to influence how analysts understand the company’s trajectory.

The first pillar of AR Strategic Maturity is narrative discipline. Immature programs rely on shifting messages, inconsistent spokespeople, and reactive storytelling. Mature programs operate from a crisp, validated narrative that analysts can easily repeat. This narrative aligns problem, audience, approach, and proof into a coherent story that holds up under scrutiny. It becomes the foundation analysts use to describe the company in research, inquiries, and buyer conversations. Narrative discipline ensures analysts understand not just what the company does, but why it matters and how it is different.

The second pillar is operational rigor. Mature AR programs run on systems, not improvisation. They maintain structured briefing calendars, evaluation readiness processes, spokesperson preparation , and cross‑functional alignment . They anticipate analyst needs, prepare executives for high‑stakes conversations, and ensure every interaction reinforces the same strategic story. Immature programs react to analyst requests; mature programs orchestrate them. This rigor reduces friction, increases analyst confidence, and ensures the company shows up consistently across every touchpoint.

The third pillar is category and market alignment. Analysts evaluate vendors through taxonomies, waves, quadrants, and segmentation frameworks that shape how markets are understood. Mature AR programs understand these frameworks deeply and position the company with precision. They know where the company fits today, where the market is moving, and how to align the narrative to analyst expectations without compromising differentiation. Immature programs try to stretch across categories or invent new ones; mature programs achieve category precision, ensuring analysts can place the company quickly and accurately.

Evidence‑backed differentiation is the fourth anchor of AR Strategic Maturity. Analysts are trained skeptics; they look for proof, not promises. Mature programs build differentiation on measurable outcomes, customer references, product capabilities, and roadmap discipline. They ensure claims are defensible, repeatable, and validated through real‑world impact. This evidence becomes the backbone of analyst confidence and the reason analysts advocate for the company in research and buyer guidance.

The final pillar is influence momentum. Mature AR programs understand that influence compounds. Every briefing , inquiry, demo, and evaluation is an opportunity to reinforce the company’s strengths and shape analyst perception. Over time, analysts begin to internalize the narrative, reference the company more frequently, and position it more favorably in research. Influence momentum is the outcome of strategic maturity, a state where analysts understand the company deeply, trust its direction, and advocate for its strengths even when the company is not in the room.

AR Strategic Maturity transforms Analyst Relations from a tactical function into a strategic advantage. It ensures the company shows up with clarity, credibility, and consistency. And, it creates the conditions for sustained analyst mindshare, stronger evaluations, and long‑term market leadership. While many vendors treat analyst interactions as one‑way broadcasts, mature organizations understand that analysts are constantly signaling what they see, what they believe, and what they need to validate a vendor’s credibility. AR Through Insights captures those signals, interprets them, and converts them into strategic advantage.

At its core, AR Through Insights reveals perception gaps - the distance between how a company sees itself and how analysts understand its value. These gaps often surface in subtle ways: the questions analysts ask, the comparisons they make, the competitors they reference, or the areas where they request more clarity. Each signal is a data point. When aggregated, they form a clear picture of where the narrative is landing and where it is not. This is the foundation of Narrative Development and a critical input to the AR Operating System.

The second dimension is competitive intelligence. Analysts often have a broader, more neutral view of the market than internal teams. Their questions and commentary reveal how competitors are positioning themselves, where they are gaining traction, and where they are struggling. AR Through Insights captures these competitive signals and translates them into strategic guidance for product, marketing, and executive teams. This intelligence helps vendors refine differentiation, strengthen claims, and anticipate competitive moves.

The third dimension is category direction. Analysts shape categories, sometimes subtly, sometimes explicitly. Their language, frameworks, and research priorities signal where the category is heading and what capabilities will matter most in the next evaluation cycle. AR Through Insights identifies these directional cues early, enabling vendors to align messaging, roadmap, and evidence long before the next MQ, Wave, or MarketScape. This is essential for Evaluation Readiness.

The fourth dimension is evidence expectations. Analysts consistently signal what proof they need to validate a vendor’s claims. They may ask for customer outcomes, product performance data, integration details, or competitive win stories. AR Through Insights captures these requests and feeds them into a structured evidence‑creation engine. This ensures the organization builds the right proof, at the right depth, with the right credibility, not generic case studies or inflated marketing claims.

The fifth dimension is organizational alignment. Analyst feedback often exposes internal misalignment: inconsistent narratives, unclear product direction, or gaps between marketing and product. AR Through Insights surfaces these issues early and provides a neutral, external lens that helps teams align around a unified story. This alignment is a core maturity signal and a prerequisite for strong analyst perception.

Finally, AR Through Insights drives intentional influence. When analyst feedback is captured, analyzed, and operationalized, AR becomes proactive rather than reactive. Vendors can anticipate questions, strengthen weak points, and deliver more strategic briefings and inquiries. Influence becomes a year‑round discipline, not a seasonal scramble. AR Through Insights is not about collecting comments, it is about converting analyst perspective into strategic clarity, competitive advantage, and measurable influence. When executed with discipline, it becomes one of the most powerful accelerators of AR maturity and market leadership.

passages.text: Impact Why a Senior‑Only Why the Traditional AR Model Falls Short - and Senior‑Only Fixes It For years, most companies have relied on a traditional Analyst Relations model: a senior AR leader supported by one or more junior practitioners who handle logistics, scheduling, reporting, and basic content preparation. On paper, this structure looks efficient. In practice, it often creates friction, slows momentum, and introduces risk into analyst interactions.

A senior‑only AR model flips that structure on its head. Instead of layering junior execution beneath senior oversight, every analyst touchpoint - every briefing, inquiry, narrative discussion, and strategic alignment moment - is led by someone with deep experience, judgment, and credibility. The difference is not subtle. It’s transformational. The Traditional AR Model: Efficient on Paper, Risky in Practice

The standard AR structure is built around leverage: senior leaders set strategy while junior staff execute. But Analyst Relations is not a function where leverage scales cleanly. Analysts are senior, time‑compressed, and highly attuned to quality. They can instantly detect when a vendor brings junior execution to the table. The traditional model often introduces: Inconsistent messaging - junior staff struggle to maintain narrative discipline across multiple analysts and firms.

Rework and corrections - briefing documents, messaging drafts, and follow‑ups often require senior rewriting. Slower progress - junior practitioners need more context, more oversight, and more iteration. Analyst frustration - analysts expect senior‑level conversations; junior‑led interactions can feel misaligned or superficial. Higher risk - a single poorly handled inquiry or briefing can damage credibility for months.

In short: the traditional model looks scalable, but it often scales inconsistency, not impact. The Senior‑Only AR Model: Precision, Credibility, and Speed A senior‑only model removes the layers that dilute quality. Every interaction is led by someone who has: 20+ years inside tech companies Experience managing analysts, evaluations, and executive narratives The judgment to adjust messaging in real time

The credibility to speak peer‑to‑peer with analysts The ability to diagnose issues quickly and act decisively This model delivers immediate advantages: 1. Higher Credibility in Every Analyst Interaction Analysts can tell within seconds whether they’re speaking with someone who understands the market, the product, and the strategic context. Senior‑only AR ensures every conversation is substantive, efficient, and aligned with analyst expectations.

2. Faster Narrative Alignment Senior practitioners don’t need layers of review or translation. They refine messaging on the fly, adjust positioning based on analyst feedback, and maintain narrative discipline across firms and touchpoints. 3. Reduced Risk and Rework No junior drafts that need rewriting. No misaligned follow‑ups. No “we’ll get back to you” moments. Senior‑only AR eliminates the operational drag that slows traditional programs.

4. Stronger Analyst Trust Analysts trust vendors who show up prepared,informed, and consistent. Senior‑only AR builds trust faster, and maintains it more reliably, because analysts know they’re always speaking with someone who understands the full picture. 5. Better Outcomes in Evaluations and Research When every interaction is senior‑led, companies see measurable improvements in: MQ and Wave positioning

Vendor Ratings Market category alignment Narrative adoption Analyst sentiment Peer review performance (GPI, G2, TrustRadius) Senior‑only AR doesn’t just feel better; it performs better. Why Senior‑Only AR Is the Future The AR landscape has changed. Analysts are stretched thin, markets are more complex, and vendors have less room for error. Companies need AR partners who can operate at the level analysts expect - not junior staff learning on the job.

A senior‑only model is: More efficient - fewer people, fewer layers, faster execution More strategic - every action ties directly to business outcomes More credible - analysts engage more deeply and more openly More predictable - fewer surprises, fewer corrections, fewer risks More impactful - better evaluations, stronger narratives, faster traction In a world where perception shapes reality, senior‑only AR is not a luxury. It’s a competitive advantage.

The Bottom Line Traditional AR models rely on leverage. Senior‑only AR relies on expertise. Traditional AR introduces risk. Senior‑only AR reduces it. Traditional AR scales activity. Senior‑only AR scales impact. If you want an AR program that moves faster, communicates more clearly, and earns analyst trust more reliably, senior‑only is the model that delivers. Visit Our Library

items.title: Competitive Positioning Analysts Respect
items.summary: Explore why analysts dismiss unsupported competitive positioning, and how disciplined responses to difficult feedback can strengthen credibility, sharpen strategy and earn lasting respect.

passages.text: Credibility Competitive Positioning Analysts Respect vs. Dismiss: The Credibility Test Strategy & Marketing Positioning Series Explore why analysts dismiss unsupported competitive positioning, and how disciplined responses to difficult feedback can strengthen credibility, sharpen strategy and earn lasting respect. Tammy Richards is a senior marketing and analyst relations leader with 25+ years of experience shaping global brands at Conga, Veeam, and Citrix. She specializes in transforming complex technology into clear, credible narratives that strengthen market position and accelerate growth. As Vice President of Operations & Delivery at Forward AR Experts, Tammy helps build a senior‑only AR firm powered by intelligence and AI - ensuring clients benefit from seasoned judgment, strategic guidance, and relationships that move the market.

Submit Your Own Article Check Out Our Library Tammy Richards Forward AR Experts VP of Operations & Delivery Tammy L. Richards | LinkedIn Why Analysts Dismiss Competitive Positioning (and What Earns Respect Instead) Every AR practitioner eventually delivers an analyst assessment that leadership doesn't want to hear: your product is behind on a capability, a competitor is perceived as stronger, the market has moved and your narrative hasn't.

What happens next determines whether the company's competitive positioning earns analyst respect or gets quietly dismissed. Too often, the internal reaction is to challenge the analyst's objectivity instead of examining the finding. That instinct is the single biggest barrier between an analyst relations program and real analyst credibility. The Competitive Positioning Credibility Test: Four Tests Analysts Apply

Analysts don't dismiss competitive claims because they're inherently skeptical. They dismiss them when the positioning fails one of four tests. Positioning that passes all four earns respect. Positioning that fails any of them gets discounted. 1. The Evidence Test Does the claim rest on proof, or on assertion? "We're the leader in X" is an assertion. "We've closed 40% more enterprise deals against Competitor Y in the last two quarters, and here's the win/loss data" is evidence. Analysts evaluate hundreds of vendors making similar claims; the ones that stand out are backed by something verifiable.

2. The Acknowledgment Test Does the claim rest on proof, or on assertion? "We're the leader in X" is an assertion. "We've closed 40% more enterprise deals against Competitor Y in the last two quarters, and here's the win/loss data" is evidence. Analysts evaluate hundreds of vendors making similar claims; the ones that stand out are backed by something verifiable.

3. The Trajectory Test Can the company show movement over time, not just a current-state snapshot? A gap that's been static for three years signals a company that isn't listening. A gap that's visibly closing, with specific milestones, signals one that acts on feedback. Analysts track vendors across cycles; trajectory is often more persuasive than any single data point.

4. The Translation Test Is the AR function translating analyst feedback into internal action, or defending the existing narrative? When AR's role gets reduced to managing the relationship rather than managing what the company does with the input, the company stops improving and starts performing. Analysts can tell. The pattern behind all four: Analysts respect positioning that treats their assessment as a mirror, not an obstacle. Positioning that argues with the mirror is what gets dismissed.

How to Build Competitive Positioning Analysts Won't Dismiss Separate the finding from your reaction to it. When an assessment lands badly, the first instinct is to relitigate methodology or question objectivity. Before doing that, ask: even if the framing is imperfect, is there a signal underneath that customers might also be picking up on? Analysts are frequently a leading indicator of market perception, not a lagging one.

Build a structured feedback loop, not a one-time readout. Translate every material finding into three categories: where you're validated, where a competitor is genuinely stronger, and what specific gap that creates. This becomes a living document product and leadership can act against, not an artifact of a single conversation. Push for milestones, not intentions. "We're aware of the gap" is not something AR can bring back to an analyst in six months. Attach real dates and scope to how a gap will close. Even directional milestones give AR something concrete to report, and give the analyst relationship a trajectory to track.

Bring competitive intelligence in before the assessment, not after. Surface competitor positioning proactively so leadership hears about a competitive gap from AR before they hear it from an analyst report. This changes the dynamic from defensive to collaborative. Run a mock evaluation before the real one. An internal mock Wave or MQ ahead of an actual evaluation cycle surfaces gaps early enough to close them before they show up in the report customers see. It also creates a baseline: compare results against the eventual real evaluation and the gap between becomes evidence of trajectory, exactly what the Trajectory Test rewards. The exercise only pays off if leadership treats it as genuine learning rather than a rehearsal for defending the existing narrative.

Protect your credibility by not overselling. If AR consistently packages every interaction as a win, leadership stops trusting AR's read on where the company actually stands. Calibrated reporting, genuine wins as wins, real gaps as gaps, is what earns AR the standing to be heard when a hard message needs to land. In Practice: When the Organization Listens vs. When It Doesn't

I've seen this pattern repeat: an analyst delivers a review with substantiated critique, and the internal reaction is to label it biased or uninformed. The opportunity to close a real gap gets lost in the effort to discredit the source. I've also seen the alternative. One organization ran a mock Wave ahead of the real cycle, inviting the same hard scrutiny on purpose. It surfaced honest gaps in a specific product and in how that product related to the broader platform story. The gaps sharpened direction rather than triggering defensiveness.

items.title: Creating A New Category
items.summary: Discover how an AR program transformed raw insights into a recognized market category, turning early signals into Revenue Lifecycle Management through strategic analyst engagement.

passages.text: AR Success - Creating a New Market Category Creating a New Market Category Analysts Can Understand and Evaluate Creating a new market category sounds impossible - until AR turns raw insights into a narrative analysts believe in. That’s the real alchemy. Move Your Business Forward AR Alchemy: Creating a Market Category Transforming Basic AR Concepts into Market Gold

In Medieval Europe, alchemy was a popular field of study among scholars, clergy, and early natural philosophers wherein attempts were made to transform base elements into valuable metals like silver and gold. It seems preposterous, but alchemy was even studied by well-known scientists such as Isaac Newton as late as the Renaissance era. In what seemed at the time like an alchemy project, in my last role I was asked to use the AR program to help the company create a new market category: Revenue Lifecycle Management (RLM). As preposterous as it sounds - transforming raw insights, emerging trends, and early product signals into a cohesive market description that feels both inevitable and groundbreaking - our alchemy project was successful. Analysts became catalysts in the process, validating the vision, crystallizing the language, and helping convert a bold idea into a recognized category.

So, how did we do it? Here is a case study… Goals and Challenges In order to achieve our golden target, we had to achieve a few goals along the way: Key influencers in our target markets (e.g., contract lifecycle management, configure price and quote, and document automation) must accept RLM as definitionally valid. Analysts must use RLM in published research to define The Company’s offering

Analyst must use RLM to define the broader category The Company must be named as the leader in the RLM category Obviously, there were some challenges we faced in order to achieve these goals, namely: The Company was the only vendor pushing RLM as a category. Only The Company offered all the components of the RLM ecosystem we had defined.

Very few end user clients were asking analysts about RLM in inquiries or searching for the term online. Building Understanding and Agreement To overcome these challenges, we established a four-step initiative to build understanding of the category definition and gain agreement from analysts that it was a valid category. With some necessary overlap in terms of timing, here were the four steps:

1) Engagement Scheduled dozens of inquiries with analysts covering CLM, CPQ, eSignature, etc. Discussed taxonomy of research in target markets, broader ERP/CRM ecosystems. Refined RLM positioning based on follow-up inquiries (e.g., describe as “middle office” offering). 2) Education Executed round of briefings and inquiries to unveil and further refine updated RLM messaging. Tailored positioning to each analysts’ individual viewpoint on RLM to gain agreement.

Some briefings (e.g., IDC) involved multiple analysts, providing invaluable collaboration. 3) Alignment Focused follow-up engagement on most influential analysts to cement alignment: Analyst 1, Gartner Analyst 2, Forrester Analyst 3&4, IDC Analyst 5, Ventana Analyst 6, 451 4) Influence Invested in webinars, speaking engagements, custom research with analysts. Focused activities in positioning CPQ, CLM, etc., in broader RLM ecosystem.

Pushed references for key evaluations that implemented multiple RLM solutions. This short list sums up more than a year of near-continual analyst engagement. Furthermore, not every briefing, inquiry, or advisory was specifically focused on building the market category. However, even in Magic Quadrant briefings, for example, we made sure to label our broad solution suite with the Revenue Lifecycle Management moniker. You have to beat the drum whenever you get the chance.

The Results It took some time for the majority of analysts to accept that our market category was valid. But, once the first crack in the dam leaked through, the water began to stronger and stronger: “[The Company] is a major player in the revenue lifecycle management space that includes CPQ and is committed to transforming and simplifying the complexities of the quote-to-revenue processes and turning them into a competitive advantage for its customers. Over the last few years, [The Company] focused on a customer-first approach companywide, made key roadmap investments, and focused on addressing key product and service issues - and it’s paying off. - Analyst #2, 2023 Forrester Wave for CPQ

“Two years ago, [The Company] rolled out what it hoped would be a new solution category - revenue lifecycle management. … Two years later, that vision has gained traction with both [The Company’s] user base and its competitors.” - May 2024 IDC Recap of The Company’s Analyst Summit 2024 “… [Company X] launched a new Revenue Lifecycle Management solution to provide deeper mid-office capabilities.” - Gartner Vendor Rating: Company X, June 2024

“Good to see [Company X] embracing Revenue Lifecycle Management (RLM), the modern version of 'quote to cash' that better reflects the realities of mixed pricing models, … . They join [The Company]] and [Company Y] marketing and selling this idea with applications.” - Analyst #5, ISG Research, June 2024 Keys to Success There really is no “magic sauce” to building a market category with AR. The reality is that it comes down to simple, “gumshoe” AR - hard work and long-term commitment. That said, there are a few important keys to success that I would highlight:

Beat the Drum - Deliver the message every time you have a chance to engage with an analyst, even it’s a “bump into” session in the hallway of an event. When the analysts think of you, the market category you’re building should be the first words that come to mind. Tailor the Message - Of course, there should be some measure of consistency in your messaging. However, every good AR pro knows that each analyst has his/her own research agenda, focus, mindset, and viewpoint. Don’t beat your head against the wall trying to convince the analysts to shift their viewpoints to fit your positioning. Instead, tailor how you position your category to fit within their taxonomy, which is the quickest way to gain traction.

items.title: Differentiation That Survives Scrutiney
items.summary: Explore how a winning AR strategy connects a differentiated narrative, the right analysts and a disciplined operating system - turning disconnected activity into consistent, measurable influence.

Gary leads senior‑level analyst relations strategy and execution for technology companies preparing for launches, evaluations, and narrative shifts. Submit Your Own Article Check Out Our Library Gary Frazier Icertis Analyst Relations Director Gary Frazier | LinkedIn Differentiation That Survives Scrutiney Differentiation That Stands Up Against Scrutiny is the discipline of building claims analysts can validate, defend, and repeat, not because they sound compelling, but because they are grounded in evidence, clarity, and competitive truth. In Analyst Relations, differentiation is not what you say that makes you unique; it is what analysts can prove that makes you unique. When your differentiation withstands questioning, comparison, and evaluation pressure, it becomes a durable competitive advantage that shapes how analysts describe you in research and buyer conversations.

Differentiation begins with precision. Analysts evaluate hundreds of vendors, and most rely on vague, inflated, or undisciplined claims. Vendors often default to the same language, “AI‑powered,” “end‑to‑end,” “unified,” “industry‑leading.” These claims collapse under scrutiny because they are not specific, measurable, or tied to outcomes. Differentiation that stands up requires stripping away generic language and articulating what you do differently, how you do it, and why it matters in a way analysts can test. Precision is the first filter analysts use to determine whether a vendor’s story is credible.

The second pillar is evidence. Analysts are trained skeptics; they look for proof, not promises. They test claims against customer outcomes, product capabilities, roadmap execution, and competitive benchmarks. Differentiation becomes real when it is backed by measurable impact: reduced cost, accelerated time to value, improved accuracy, increased automation, stronger security posture, or higher customer satisfaction. When your differentiation is supported by repeatable, verifiable outcomes, analysts begin to internalize your strengths and reference them confidently. Evidence transforms differentiation from marketing language into analyst‑validated truth.

Competitive clarity is the third anchor of differentiation that withstands scrutiny. Analysts constantly compare vendors - feature by feature, capability by capability, outcome by outcome. If your differentiation cannot be articulated in contrast to alternatives, it will not hold. This does not mean attacking competitors; it means defining your unique approach, methodology, architecture, or value model in a way that is distinct and defensible. Analysts reward vendors who understand the competitive landscape and can clearly articulate where they excel, where they are different, and where they are intentionally not competing. This clarity builds trust and positions you as a mature, self‑aware player.

Differentiation also requires consistency across every analyst touchpoint. Analysts test your claims in briefings , inquiries, demos, customer reference calls, and evaluations. If your story shifts, expands, or contradicts itself across these interactions, analysts lose confidence. Differentiation that stands up is reinforced through disciplined messaging, aligned teams, and a narrative that holds under pressure. When analysts see consistency between what you say and what you deliver, they begin to repeat your differentiation in their own language, which is the ultimate sign of influence .

Over time, differentiation that withstands scrutiny becomes a compounding asset . Analysts begin to use your strengths as benchmarks in research. Your capabilities become reference points in evaluations. Your outcomes become examples in buyer conversations. Competitors are measured against you rather than the other way around. This is the moment when differentiation becomes market power.

When differentiation is weak, vague, or unproven, analysts default to competitors with clearer, stronger, or more credible stories. This leads to weaker evaluations, fewer mentions, and diminished influence in high‑value buying cycles. Differentiation That Stands Up Against Scrutiny ensures analysts can validate your claims, defend your strengths, and advocate for your value, even when you’re not in the room.

Submit Your Own Article Check Out Our Library Gary Frazier Icertis Analyst Relations Director Gary Frazier | LinkedIn Executive Influence Executive Influence is the highest expression of leadership impact within Analyst Relations, the point where executives no longer simply participate in analyst conversations but actively shape how analysts understand the company’s strategy, differentiation, and long‑term trajectory . It is the shift from presence to persuasion, from visibility to authority, from participation to market‑shaping influence. Executive Influence ensures analysts see the company through the lens of strong, aligned, strategically fluent leadership.

Executive Influence begins with strategic clarity. Analysts expect leaders to articulate the company’s direction with precision: where the market is going, how the company is positioned, and why its approach is differentiated. When executives speak with clarity and conviction, analysts interpret it as evidence of organizational maturity and strategic discipline. When leaders struggle to articulate the story, analysts assume internal misalignment. passages.text: Restore Your Analyst Relationships A Gartner Peer Insights Success Case Study: From Pretender to Pacesetter This engagement delivered a measurable shift in analyst perception - strengthening category clarity, elevating customer‑validated proof points, and driving a marked increase in positive analyst sentiment across key evaluations. Move Forward How We Transformed Our Gartner Peer Insights Performance If you are involved in sourced peer reviews for technology markets, you are undoubtedly aware of Gartner Peer Insights (GPI). GPI was launched by Gartner in 2015 as an alternative to review platforms such as G2 and TrustRadius and (as with most things Gartner-related) soon dominated the market - hosting more than 850,000 reviews and ratings across nearly 400 markets covering 7,500 providers and more than 11,600 products.

The importance of peer review sites like GPI is hard to overestimate. According to a 2024 Wynter survey of 100 B2B SaaS marketing leaders, 81% of buyers check third-party review sites when vetting software. Additionally, Starsight Communications found in 2023 that 95% of B2B buyers read online reviews to shortlist vendors. Depending on the focus of your company, as well as the emphasis placed on it by certain Gartner analysts, GPI can play an important role in your analyst relations program as well. This was the case when I recently accepted a role as AR Director and found the company ranked in the middle of the pack (at best) in our markets on GPI.

Working in close collaboration with an amazing Customer Advocacy team, and with full strategic and financial support from the CEO, we revitalized the company’s GPI program and ultimately found ourselves at the top of the rankings! Keep reading to find out how we did it. Goals and Challenges Challenges Lack of focus on GPI left the company lagging competitors in number of reviews and overall rating in key markets.

There was a limited number of referenceable customers. Most referenceable customers were dedicated to other incentivized activities. Introduction of new Voice of the Customer (VoC) reports left little time to plan and execute a sourcing strategy. Goals Crank up the Volume - Take the lead in number of reviews Shoot for the Stars - Focus on customers who would provide 5-star reviews

Impact Key Reports - Meet key milestones to impact our standing in both Magic Quadrant and VoC reports Ultimately, achieve “Customer Choice” ranking in VoC reports The Solution There are so many factors other than GPI ratings that impact the analysis of companies for the Magic Quadrant. So, while we knew our efforts would have a positive impact on our MQ standing, we focused the strategy where it would have the greatest impact: inclusion, and ultimately Customer Choice ranking, in the Voice of the Customer reports.

With this in mind, we had to get enough reviews to meet the volume criteria for inclusion (i.e., 20+ eligible reviews in the 18-month window). We also had to push for reviews that positively impacted both axes on the chart: User Adoption and Interest Reviews + Considerations Willingness to Recommend Market Coverage Overall Experience Overall Rating

Service & Support Product Capabilities With a finite amount of time and limited funds from Gartner for customer incentives, we elected to incentivize employees instead via a SPIFF. We wanted to focus on employees who had the closest relationships with our customers and would therefore know who was likely to provide the best scores in these target areas. However, in the long run, we chose to offer incentives to any employee who could generate the reviews we needed. As a result, we found that our Tech Support team was far and away our greatest resource for reviews!

Here’s where it gets tricky. Gartner makes it impossible to tie individual reviews to specific customers. So, without opening up the kimono too far, we were able to create GPI campaigns in such a way that we could logically estimate how many published reviews a specific employee had generated and reward them accordingly. The strategy wasn’t completely employee-focused, however. We also shifted our efforts on driving customer reviews to GPI at our user conference, where previously the efforts had been focused on G2 and TrustRadius.

Needless to say, the results were overwhelmingly positive as we generated significantly more reviews than we needed. And, the ratings greatly increased our rankings across the board. The Results In both markets, our # of reviews moved from 5th to 1st! In one market, # of reviews increased 6x YoY, and our overall rating jumped from 3.7 to 4.3 out of 5 stars.

In the same market, we qualified for the Voice of the Customer for the first time. In the latest edition, our company was ranked as “Customer Choice” in the report. In another market, our review increased 68% YoY and our overall rating jumped from 4.1 to 4.6 out of 5 stars. In that same market, our company was the sole “Customer Choice” vendor in the inaugural Voice of the Customer report and continued that standing in the next edition.

It’s hard to quantify what impact these results had on the company’s dot placement in the associated Magic Quadrant reports. However, in one market, the mentions of customer reviews in the company profile went from being highlighted in the “Cautions” to being highlighted in the “Strengths.” Keys to Success As anyone who has executed a Gartner Peer Insights strategy knows, there is no magic formula that will work for everyone company and every market. However, here are a few basic principles I would recommend to achieve the best success:

Teamwork, Teamwork, Teamwork - No man is an island when it comes to AR in general, but especially as it relates to Gartner Peer Insights. Maintain close ties with your Customer Advocacy team. You want to help mold the strategy but allow them to do their work executing it. If you don’t have a good CA team, build a tiger team with Sales, Customer Success, and Marketing to build a strong stable of positive customer references.

Submit Your Own Article Visit Our Library Gary Frazier Icertis Analyst Relations Director Gary Frazier | LinkedIn Forward AR Strategy Market Positioning AR Strategy & Market Positioning is the foundation of how analysts understand your company, categorize your offerings, and evaluate your competitive strength. It is not a messaging exercise; it is a strategic discipline that determines how effectively you compete in markets shaped by analyst frameworks, taxonomies, and evaluation criteria. When your positioning aligns with analyst expectations , you reduce friction, strengthen credibility, and create a narrative that analysts can confidently repeat to buyers, peers, and other analysts.

Strong positioning begins with narrative clarity. Analysts must immediately understand the problem you solve, the audience you serve, and the differentiated approach that sets you apart. Vendors often underestimate how quickly analysts form mental models. If your story is unclear, overly broad, or misaligned with market realities, analysts struggle to place you. This leads to misinterpretation, weaker evaluations, and missed opportunities for inclusion in research. A crisp, disciplined narrative becomes the anchor analysts use to describe your value in conversations and reports. And, it becomes the lens through which they interpret your roadmap, customer outcomes, and competitive posture.

Category alignment is the second pillar of effective AR positioning. Analysts define markets through structured taxonomies, waves, quadrants, and segmentation frameworks that influence how vendors are compared. When your positioning fits cleanly into these structures, analysts can evaluate you accurately and consistently. When it doesn’t, you create unnecessary friction. Vendors often attempt to “ create a new category ,” but analysts prioritize buyer demand, market maturity, and comparative frameworks. The goal is not to invent a category; it is to achieve category precision, ensuring your placement reflects where the market is going and how analysts already think about the space.

Evidence‑backed differentiation is the third anchor. Analysts are not persuaded by adjectives or aspirational messaging; they are persuaded by proof. Customer outcomes, product capabilities, roadmap discipline, and measurable traction form the backbone of credibility. When your evidence reinforces your narrative, analysts internalize your strengths and begin to repeat them. This is where positioning becomes a competitive advantage. Analysts start using your language to describe market trends, benchmarking competitors against your capabilities, and interpreting your momentum through a lens of confidence rather than skepticism.

Over time, strong positioning creates a compounding effect . Your story becomes the default mental model for your category. Your strengths become the reference points others must match. Your roadmap is viewed as intentional and credible. Your inclusion in evaluations becomes more consistent. Analysts reference you more frequently in research and buyer conversations. This compounding influence is one of the most powerful outcomes of disciplined Analyst Relations.

Poor positioning, by contrast, creates costly downstream effects. Analysts may miscategorize you, undervalue your strengths, or misunderstand your differentiation, not because your product is weak, but because your story is unclear or misaligned. This misalignment can lead to weaker evaluations, fewer research mentions, and diminished influence in high‑value buying cycles. A winning AR positioning strategy aligns narrative, category, and evidence into a cohesive, analyst‑ready story that holds up under scrutiny. It ensures your messaging is consistent across briefings , demos, customer references, and roadmap discussions. It positions you for long‑term relevance, stronger evaluations, and sustained market leadership.

items.title: The Maturity Signals Analyst Look For
items.summary: Explore the signals analysts use to assess organizational maturity - from leadership clarity and market positioning to customer evidence, operational discipline and consistent execution.

passages.text: Currency that drives influence The Maturity Signals Analyst Look For Program Excellence Series Explore the signals analysts use to assess organizational maturity - from leadership clarity and market positioning to customer evidence, operational discipline and consistent execution. Currency That Drives Influence The Maturity Signals Analyst Look For The Maturity Signals Analysts Look For are the operational cues , behavioral patterns, and execution markers that tell analysts whether a vendor is credible, aligned, and ready to lead. Analysts don’t evaluate maturity based on marketing polish or executive charisma; they evaluate it through consistency, clarity, and the repeatability of how a company shows up. These signals shape analyst perception long before an evaluation begins - and they determine whether analysts view a vendor as a rising leader or an organization still finding its footi

The first maturity signal is narrative discipline. Analysts expect vendors to articulate a crisp, defensible story that explains what the company does, why it matters, and how it delivers measurable outcomes. When every executive, product leader, and spokesperson reinforces the same narrative, analysts interpret it as organizational alignment. When messages drift, contradict, or shift depending on the audience, analysts assume internal confusion. Narrative discipline is the foundation of maturity and directly connects to Narrative Development and Strategic Clarity.

The second signal is evidence strength. Analysts are trained skeptics ; they look for proof, not promises. Mature vendors bring customer outcomes, product performance data, competitive wins, and measurable impact to every interaction. They avoid inflated claims and instead rely on validated evidence that stands up under scrutiny . Weak or inconsistent evidence signals immaturity, while strong, repeatable proof signals operational strength. This is a core component of Evidence‑Backed Differentiation.

The third signal is execution consistency. Analysts pay close attention to how vendors operate - not just what they say. Missed deadlines, shifting roadmaps, inconsistent spokesperson performance, or last‑minute evaluation scrambles all signal operational instability. Mature vendors demonstrate predictable execution: they prepare early, respond quickly, and show up consistently strong across briefings, inquiries, and evaluations. Consistency is one of the most powerful indicators of maturity because it reflects the underlying health of the organization.

The fourth signal is category precision. Analysts expect vendors to understand where they fit, how the category is evolving, and what differentiates them within it. Immature vendors stretch across categories, invent new ones, or rely on vague positioning. Mature vendors demonstrate clarity: they know the category boundaries, the competitive landscape, and the analyst frameworks that shape perception. Category precision helps analysts place the vendor accurately and confidently - a critical factor in evaluations like the MQ and Wave .

The fifth signal is executive fluency . Analysts look for leaders who can articulate strategy, market direction, and product vision with confidence and depth. Executives who rely on scripts or struggle to answer probing questions signal immaturity. Executives who demonstrate command of the business, transparency about limitations, and clarity about direction signal strength. This is where Executive Influence becomes a defining maturity marker.

The final signal is year‑round readiness. Mature vendors don’t treat evaluations as seasonal events. They maintain readiness across narrative, evidence, references, and product clarity throughout the year. Analysts notice when a vendor is always prepared - and they reward it with trust, stronger perception, and more favorable positioning . Together, these maturity signals shape how analysts understand a vendor’s credibility, stability, and long‑term potential. When vendors demonstrate these signals consistently, they earn analyst confidence - and confidence is the currency that drives influence, evaluation performance, and market leadership.
